The AND function returns TRUE if all of its arguments evaluate to TRUE, and returns FALSE if one or more arguments evaluate to FALSE; its syntax is AND(logical1, [logical2], ...), and it is commonly used as the logical_test argument of IF to test more than one condition at once.
The OR function returns TRUE if any of its arguments evaluate to TRUE, and returns FALSE if all of its arguments evaluate to FALSE; its syntax is OR(logical1, [logical2], ...).
Text in formulas goes in quotes; for example =IF(A2>B2,"Over Budget","OK") tests whether A2 is greater than B2 and returns one of the two quoted text results.
A nested IF can convert a numeric score to a letter grade, for example =IF(D2>89,"A",IF(D2>79,"B",IF(D2>69,"C",IF(D2>59,"D","F")))).

briefs.learning_objective: Combine several text values into one string using TEXTJOIN or CONCATENATE, inserting a delimiter between the joined values.

required_facts.statement: TEXTJOIN combines text from multiple ranges or strings and inserts a delimiter you specify between each text value; its syntax is TEXTJOIN(delimiter, ignore_empty, text1, [text2], ...).
In TEXTJOIN, setting the ignore_empty argument to TRUE skips empty cells among the arguments rather than joining them in as blank values.

CONCATENATE joins two or more text strings into one string; its syntax is CONCATENATE(text1, [text2], ...), though Microsoft recommends using the newer CONCAT function instead, since CONCATENATE may not be available in future versions of Excel.

briefs.learning_objective: Extract a substring from fixed positions in a text value using LEFT, RIGHT, or MID, and remove extra spaces using TRIM.

required_facts.statement: LEFT returns the first character or characters in a text string, based on the number of characters you specify; its syntax is LEFT(text, [num_chars]).
RIGHT returns the last character or characters in a text string, based on the number of characters you specify; its syntax is RIGHT(text, [num_chars]).
MID returns a specific number of characters from a text string, starting at the position you specify; its syntax is MID(text, start_num, num_chars).
TRIM removes all spaces from a text value except for single spaces between words; its syntax is TRIM(text).

briefs.learning_objective: Compute a date-based value, such as an age in years, using TODAY together with DATEDIF.

required_facts.statement: The TODAY function returns the serial number of the current date and takes no arguments; its syntax is TODAY().

The DATEDIF function returns the difference between a start_date and an end_date in the unit you specify; its syntax is DATEDIF(start_date, end_date, unit), where a unit of "Y" returns the number of complete years in the period.
DATEDIF is useful in formulas where you need to calculate an age.
Excel stores dates as sequential serial numbers so they can be used in calculations; by default, January 1, 1900 is serial number 1.
DATEDIF's unit argument "D" returns the number of days in the period between start_date and end_date.

briefs.learning_objective: Aggregate only the rows that match one or more conditions using COUNTIF, COUNTIFS, SUMIF, or SUMIFS.

required_facts.statement: COUNTIF counts the number of cells in a range that meet a single criterion; its syntax is COUNTIF(range, criteria).

COUNTIFS applies criteria to cells across multiple ranges and counts the number of times all the criteria are met together; its syntax is COUNTIFS(criteria_range1, criteria1, [criteria_range2, criteria2], ...), and each additional range must have the same number of rows and columns as criteria_range1.

SUMIF sums the values in a range that meet criteria you specify, optionally applying the criteria to one range while summing the corresponding values in a different range; its syntax is SUMIF(range, criteria, [sum_range]).

SUMIFS adds the cells in a sum_range that meet multiple criteria at once, where each criteria_range/criteria pair is a separate condition that must all be met; its syntax is SUMIFS(sum_range, criteria_range1, criteria1, [criteria_range2, criteria2], ...).

Criteria for these functions can be a number, expression, cell reference, or text, such as 32, ">32", B4, or "apples"; criteria containing comparison symbols or text must be enclosed in quotation marks.
The same range can be used in more than one criteria pair to test a range condition, for example =COUNTIFS(A2:A7,"<6",A2:A7,">1") counts values between 1 and 6.

briefs.learning_objective: Write a VLOOKUP or XLOOKUP formula that finds a key in a table and returns a corresponding value from another column.

required_facts.statement: VLOOKUP looks up a value in the leftmost column of a range and returns a value from the same row in a column you specify by its position; its syntax is VLOOKUP(lookup_value, table_array, col_index_num, [range_lookup]).

In VLOOKUP, entering FALSE (or 0) for range_lookup searches for an exact match to lookup_value; leaving range_lookup blank or entering TRUE searches for an approximate match instead, and TRUE is the default if the argument is omitted.

HLOOKUP works like VLOOKUP but searches across the top row of a table and returns a value from a row you specify by its position; its syntax is HLOOKUP(lookup_value, table_array, row_index_num, [range_lookup]).

XLOOKUP searches lookup_array for lookup_value and returns the corresponding item from return_array, producing an exact match by default; its syntax is XLOOKUP(lookup_value, lookup_array, return_array, [if_not_found], [match_mode], [search_mode]).
VLOOKUP can only look up a value from left to right, but XLOOKUP works in any direction and returns exact matches by default.
source_refs: excel_vlookup_index_match_guide#Using INDEX and MATCH instead of VLOOKUP

briefs.learning_objective: Combine INDEX and MATCH to look up a value when the return column is not to the right of the key column.

required_facts.statement: MATCH searches for a specified item in a range of cells and returns the relative position of that item within the range; its syntax is MATCH(lookup_value, lookup_array, [match_type]).

Setting MATCH's match_type to 0 finds an exact match; a match_type of 1, or omitting the argument, finds the largest value that is less than or equal to lookup_value, and requires lookup_array to be sorted in ascending order.
INDEX returns the value of an element in a range or array, selected by its row and column position; the array form's syntax is INDEX(array, row_num, [column_num]).

VLOOKUP can only look up a value from left to right, meaning the column containing the lookup value must be to the left of the column containing the return value; when the layout isn't built that way, MATCH can find the row position of the key and INDEX can then return the value from any column at that row position.
source_refs: excel_vlookup_index_match_guide#Using INDEX and MATCH instead of VLOOKUP

briefs.learning_objective: Given a formula's error value, diagnose which class of problem — a failed lookup, an invalid reference, or a wrong data type — is causing it.

required_facts.statement: The #N/A error generally indicates that a formula can't find what it's been asked to look for; the most common cause is with XLOOKUP, VLOOKUP, HLOOKUP, LOOKUP, or MATCH functions when the lookup value doesn't exist in the source data.
The #REF! error shows when a formula refers to a cell that's not valid, which happens most often when cells that were referenced by formulas get deleted or pasted over.
#VALUE! is Excel's way of saying there's something wrong with the way a formula is typed, or something wrong with the cells it's referencing.

A formula like =A1+B1+C1 can break and return a #VALUE! error if any of the referenced cells contains a non-numeric (text) value, whereas a SUM formula over the same cells ignores the text values and sums only the numeric ones.
If AVERAGE or SUM refer to cells that contain #VALUE! errors, the formulas will result in a #VALUE! error.

briefs.learning_objective: Build a PivotTable that places one field in Rows, another in Columns, and a numeric field in Values.

required_facts.statement: A PivotTable is a tool to calculate, summarize, and analyze data that lets you see comparisons, patterns, and trends in your data.
source_refs: excel_pivottable_guide#Create a PivotTable to analyze worksheet data

required_facts.statement: To create a PivotTable, select the data cells, select Insert > PivotTable, choose where to place the PivotTable report, and select OK.
source_refs: excel_pivottable_guide#Create a PivotTable in Excel for Windows

required_facts.statement: To add a field to the PivotTable, select its checkbox in the PivotTable Fields pane; selected fields are added to their default areas, with non-numeric fields added to Rows and numeric fields added to Values, and a field can be moved to a different area by dragging it there.

Filters area fields are shown as top-level report filters above the PivotTable; Columns area fields are shown as Column Labels at the top of the PivotTable; Rows area fields are shown as Row Labels on the left side of the PivotTable; Values area fields are shown as summarized numeric values in the PivotTable.

briefs.learning_objective: Change a PivotTable value field's summary function, recognizing that Sum is the default for numeric fields.

required_facts.statement: Data in a PivotTable's Values area summarizes the underlying source data by default using the SUM function for numeric values and the COUNT function for text values.
source_refs: excel_pivottable_summary_guide#Change the summary function or custom calculation for a field in a PivotTable

required_facts.statement: To change a value field's summary function, select the field in the Values area, on the PivotTable Analyze tab select Active Field > Field Settings (or right-click the value and choose Value Field Settings), select the Summarize Values By tab, and choose the summary function you want, such as Average.

briefs.learning_objective: Build a bar chart from a summary table, arranging category and value data in columns or rows before inserting the chart.

required_facts.statement: Bar charts illustrate comparisons among individual items; in a bar chart, the categories are typically organized along one axis and the values along the other.

To create a chart, select the data for the chart, select Insert > Recommended Charts, and select a chart on the Recommended Charts tab to preview it; if you don't see a bar chart you like, select the All Charts tab to see all chart types, select the chart, and select OK.
source_refs: excel_create_chart_guide#Create a chart from start to finish

briefs.learning_objective: Build a line chart from time-ordered data to show a trend across the sequence.

required_facts.statement: In a line chart, category data is distributed evenly along the horizontal axis and value data along the vertical axis; line charts can show continuous data over time on an evenly scaled axis, making them well suited to showing trends at equal intervals such as months, quarters, or fiscal years.

To create a chart, select the data for the chart, select Insert > Recommended Charts, and select a chart on the Recommended Charts tab to preview it; if you don't see a line chart you like, select the All Charts tab to see all chart types, select the chart, and select OK.
source_refs: excel_create_chart_guide#Create a chart from start to finish

briefs.learning_objective: Build a pie chart that shows each category's share of a single total.

required_facts.statement: Pie charts show the size of items in one data series proportional to the sum of the items, and are appropriate when you have only one data series to plot, none of the values are negative, there are no more than seven categories, and the categories represent parts of the whole pie.

To create a chart, select the data for the chart, select Insert > Recommended Charts, and select a chart on the Recommended Charts tab to preview it; if you don't see a pie chart you like, select the All Charts tab to see all chart types, select the chart, and select OK.
source_refs: excel_create_chart_guide#Create a chart from start to finish

briefs.learning_objective: Given a description of an experiment, identify its control group, its treatment group, and the metric being compared between them.

required_facts.statement: Studies where researchers assign treatments to cases are called experiments; when the assignment includes randomization, it is called a randomized experiment.
Researchers randomly assign cases to a control group and a treatment group so that differences between the groups that cannot otherwise be controlled are evened out.

A/B testing works by showing two variants of a page or experience to users at random: the original (control, or A) and a modified version (variation, or B); engagement with each version is measured and then compared against the baseline, the control.

briefs.learning_objective: Compute and interpret the lift (percentage change) between a treatment group's result and a control group's result.

required_facts.statement: Relative improvement (lift) is the percentage difference in the variation's conversion rate over the baseline (control) conversion rate; for example, a 10% relative improvement over a 25% baseline conversion rate means the variation's conversion rate is 27.5%.
Relative improvement describes the variation's change as a percentage of the baseline's rate.
Analyzing an A/B test's results means determining whether the variation had a positive, negative, or neutral effect compared with the baseline (control).

briefs.learning_objective: Given two results with the same estimate but different sample sizes, explain why the estimate from the larger sample is more trustworthy.

required_facts.statement: A bigger sample tends to provide a more precise point estimate than a smaller sample.

The more cases researchers observe, the more accurately they can estimate the effect of the explanatory variable on the response; in a single study, this is done by collecting a sufficiently large sample.

optional_enrichment.statement: When talking about the variability of a point estimate, such as a sample proportion, the term standard error is typically used rather than standard deviation.

briefs.learning_objective: Given a result reported with a significance or confidence figure, explain what that figure does and doesn't tell you about the underlying effect.

required_facts.statement: The null hypothesis (H0) often represents a skeptical position or a perspective of "no difference", and the alternative hypothesis (HA) represents an alternative claim under consideration.

The p-value is the probability of observing data at least as favorable to the alternative hypothesis as our current data set, if the null hypothesis were true; it is used to quantify the strength of evidence against the null hypothesis.

Statistical significance is a measure of how unusual an experiment's results would be if there were actually no difference in performance between the variation and the baseline and the discrepancy were due to random chance alone.

A confidence interval represents a range of plausible values where we are likely to find the population parameter; if many samples were taken and a 95% confidence interval were built from each one, about 95% of those intervals would contain the parameter.

Describing a confidence interval as capturing the population parameter with a certain probability is a common error; while it may be useful to think of it that way, the confidence level only quantifies how plausible it is that the parameter is in the given interval.

When the sample size becomes large, even a very small, practically unimportant difference can be detected and called statistically significant; such a difference is statistically significant but not practically significant.

misconceptions.statement: Not every confidence interval captures the true population proportion: in an illustrative set of twenty-five 95% confidence intervals built from different samples (around p = 0.88), only one failed to contain the population proportion, showing that a small fraction of intervals will miss it even when the method is followed correctly.

briefs.learning_objective: Given an experiment's results, state a business conclusion that follows from the data without overreaching beyond what the numbers show.

required_facts.statement: The null hypothesis (H0) often represents a skeptical perspective or a claim to be tested, and the alternative hypothesis (HA) represents an alternative claim under consideration; the value being compared to the parameter in this setup is called the null value.

In one hypothesis-test example, because the null value (p0 = 0.333) fell within the confidence interval computed from the sample, that value was not implausible, so the data did not provide sufficient evidence to reject the null hypothesis.

In a second example, the null value (p0 = 0.333) was not in the 95% confidence interval, so the null hypothesis was rejected: the data provided statistically significant evidence that the proportion differed from 0.333, and because the entire interval was below 0.333, it was concluded to be lower.
Analyzing an A/B test's results means determining whether the variation had a positive, negative, or neutral effect compared with the baseline (control).

When the sample size becomes large, even a very small, practically unimportant difference can be detected and called statistically significant; for example, an online experiment might find that placing additional ads on a movie review website statistically significantly increases viewership of a TV show by 0.001%, but this increase might not have any practical value.

While we failed to reject the null hypothesis in the first example, that does not necessarily mean the null hypothesis is true; perhaps there was an actual difference, but we were not able to detect it with the relatively small sample of 50.

misconceptions.statement: Failing to reject the null hypothesis is not equivalent to accepting the null hypothesis as true; it only means there was not strong enough evidence for the alternative.

briefs.learning_objective: Recognize matplotlib's Figure/Axes object model: identify which calls create the Figure vs. the Axes, and create a Figure with one Axes to plot on.

required_facts.statement: Matplotlib graphs data on Figures, and each Figure can contain one or more Axes, which is the area where data is actually plotted.
fig, ax = plt.subplots() creates a Figure and one Axes together, giving explicit variables for both objects.
Plotting calls such as ax.plot(x, y) draw onto that specific Axes object.

briefs.learning_objective: Adjust a matplotlib figure's size using figsize and its subplot spacing using tight_layout so a plot renders clearly without overlapping labels.

required_facts.statement: plt.subplots(figsize=(width, height)) sets the figure's dimensions; figsize is a (width, height) tuple which is interpreted as (width, height, 'in'), and its default is rcParams['figure.figsize'], which defaults to [6.4, 4.8].
tight_layout() automatically adjusts subplot parameters so that the subplot(s) fit into the figure area; it works by checking the extents of tick labels, axis labels, and titles.
tight_layout() can be called as plt.tight_layout() or fig.tight_layout().

optional_enrichment.statement: layout='constrained' is an alternative to tight_layout() that automatically adjusts subplots so decorations like tick labels, legends, and colorbars do not overlap, and is more flexible for cases such as colorbars on multiple axes.

briefs.learning_objective: Create a basic plot from data using matplotlib's pyplot interface, with the correct plt.plot() argument form.

required_facts.statement: plt.plot(y) called with a single array argument treats it as the y-values and automatically generates the x-values starting from 0.
plt.plot(x, y) called with two array arguments plots the y-values against the given x-values.

briefs.learning_objective: Create a bar chart with matplotlib to compare a numeric value across discrete categories, aligning bars to a common baseline.

required_facts.statement: plt.bar(x, height) (or ax.bar(x, height)) makes a bar plot with bars positioned at the given x coordinates and given heights, with the baseline defaulting to 0.
A bar chart is a common chart type for graphing categorical data or data sorted into groups.
Bar charts are easy to interpret because the eye is good at comparing lengths when the objects being compared are aligned to a common baseline.
Categorical variables such as names can be passed directly as the x argument to plt.bar() (for example plt.bar(names, values)), rather than only numeric x-positions.

misconceptions.statement: A bar's baseline can start at any value without distorting the comparison.

briefs.learning_objective: Create a histogram with matplotlib to visualize a numeric variable's distribution, and adjust the bins parameter to change how the data is binned.

required_facts.statement: plt.hist(x, bins=...) uses numpy.histogram to bin the data in x, count the number of values in each bin, and draw the result as bars.

The bins parameter defaults to rcParams['hist.bins'], which defaults to 10; passing an integer sets that many equal-width bins, passing a sequence sets explicit bin edges, and passing a string such as 'auto' selects a binning strategy.

briefs.learning_objective: Create a line plot with matplotlib to visualize a trend in a numeric value over an ordered sequence such as time.

required_facts.statement: Line graphs are best when you want to show how the value of something changes over time, or compare how several things change over time relative to each other.
plt.plot(x, y) plots the y-values against the given x-values.
A line graph plots the measured points and then draws a line that connects those points, making it easier to see how the values rose, fell, or stayed the same over time.

briefs.learning_objective: Create a scatter plot with matplotlib to visualize the relationship between two numeric variables.

required_facts.statement: plt.scatter(x, y) (or ax.scatter(x, y)) makes a scatter plot of the y-values against the x-values, one point per (x, y) pair.
A scatterplot shows the relationship between two numerical variables plotted simultaneously along the horizontal and vertical axis, and is useful for focusing on the relationship between two series.

briefs.learning_objective: Create a box plot with matplotlib to visualize a numeric variable's quartiles, median, and outliers, optionally comparing several groups.

required_facts.statement: plt.boxplot(x) (or ax.boxplot(x)) draws a box plot from the data in x; it accepts array-like data and can draw one or more boxes.

The box extends from the first quartile (Q1) to the third quartile (Q3) of the data, with a line at the median. The whiskers extend from the box to the farthest data point lying within 1.5x the interquartile range (IQR) from the box; points past the end of the whiskers are flier points (outliers).
Boxplots offer a condensed display for comparing the distributions of multiple datasets side by side.
Passing a sequence of 1D arrays as x draws one box for each array in the sequence; tick_labels=[...] labels each boxplot's tick accordingly instead of leaving it as a numeric value.

briefs.learning_objective: Add a title, axis labels, and a legend to a matplotlib plot so it is understandable on its own.

required_facts.statement: ax.set_xlabel('...') and ax.set_ylabel('...') set the x-axis and y-axis labels, and ax.set_title('...') sets the Axes title.
Passing label='...' to a plotting call (e.g. ax.plot(data, label='data1')) and then calling ax.legend() displays a legend identifying each labeled series.
In the pyplot interface, plt.xlabel(), plt.ylabel(), and plt.title() set the same label/title elements on the current Axes.

briefs.learning_objective: Match a chart type (bar, histogram, line, scatter, or box) to the analytical question being explored during one's own analysis.

required_facts.statement: A bar chart is used for graphing categorical data and comparing values across categories.
plt.hist() bins a numeric variable, counts values per bin, and draws the distribution as bars.
Line graphs are best when you want to show how a value changes over time, or compare how several things change over time relative to each other.
A scatterplot shows the relationship between two numerical variables plotted along the horizontal and vertical axis.
Boxplots offer a condensed display for comparing the distributions of multiple datasets side by side.

briefs.learning_objective: Plot directly from a pandas DataFrame's columns with seaborn by passing the DataFrame via data= and the column names via x=/y=, instead of extracting arrays first.

required_facts.statement: Seaborn's plotting functions operate on dataframes and arrays containing whole datasets, taking only the names of the variables and their roles in the plot (for example data=, x=, y=) rather than requiring the caller to extract each array.

seaborn.barplot(data=..., x=..., y=...) visualizes an aggregate statistical estimate for each category as a bar; its default estimator is the mean, and it draws an error bar (uncertainty indicator) around each bar by default.

briefs.learning_objective: Use a seaborn statistical plotting function to visualize a statistical relationship, such as a fitted trend between two numeric variables, directly from the data.

required_facts.statement: Many seaborn functions will automatically perform the statistical estimation necessary to answer questions such as the average value of one variable as a function of other variables.
seaborn.regplot(data=..., x=..., y=...) plots a scatterplot of the observations together with a fitted linear regression line.

briefs.learning_objective: Apply one of seaborn's built-in themes and a color palette to a plot using sns.set_theme().

required_facts.statement: sns.set_theme(style=..., palette=...) changes the global defaults for all plots using the matplotlib rcParams system, so it affects matplotlib plots too, even ones not made with seaborn.

seaborn.set_theme() accepts a style parameter (default 'darkgrid') and a palette parameter (default 'deep') among its arguments, which set the plot's background/gridline style and its color palette respectively.

briefs.learning_objective: Apply custom styling beyond seaborn's built-in themes, using a matplotlib style sheet or rcParams, and set a custom color palette with seaborn.

required_facts.statement: plt.style.use('style-name') applies one of matplotlib's predefined style sheets (for example 'ggplot' or 'dark_background'); the available styles can be listed with plt.style.available.
source_refs: matplotlib_official_docs#Customizing Matplotlib with style sheets and rcParams

required_facts.statement: A custom style file can set specific properties, such as 'axes.titlesize', 'lines.linewidth', or tick label sizes, and rcParams (for example mpl.rcParams['lines.linewidth'] = 2) can be set directly to change defaults globally.
source_refs: matplotlib_official_docs#Customizing Matplotlib with style sheets and rcParams

required_facts.statement: seaborn.set_palette(palette, ...) sets the matplotlib color cycle from a seaborn palette, applying that color scheme to subsequent plots.

briefs.learning_objective: Lay out multiple related plots in one figure using a grid of subplots.

required_facts.statement: fig, axs = plt.subplots(nrows, ncols) creates a Figure containing a grid of Axes with the given number of rows and columns (for example plt.subplots(2, 2) creates a 2x2 grid).
Each Axes in the returned grid is indexed separately (for example axs[0, 0]) and plotting/labeling calls made on one Axes only affect that panel.

briefs.learning_objective: Identify the business decision that a stakeholder's analysis request is meant to inform.

required_facts.statement: Analysis is the collection, manipulation and interpretation of information and data for use in decision-making.
The engagement and scoping stage of an analytical project should establish an understanding of how the analysis will inform decisions.

briefs.learning_objective: State an analysis finding as a specific, complete claim that accurately reflects what the data shows, rather than a vague summary.

required_facts.statement: A communication's big idea must articulate a unique point of view, convey what's at stake, and be a complete sentence.

A claim about the data should be checked against what the data actually shows, and narrowed if needed; one article's example revises the broader claim 'Price has declined for all products' to the more precise 'the average retail price of existing products declined' once the underlying data was examined more closely.
Writing about data should be specific about the point being made.

Putting data into context includes making comparisons, for example: 'There were 787,000 suspensions in the 2022/23 academic year. This is an increase from the previous year, when 578,300 suspensions occurred...'

optional_enrichment.statement: The communication of an analysis should be quality assured in a proportionate manner to ensure an accurate reflection of the analytical results.

briefs.learning_objective: Convert a vague business question into a specific analytical question with agreed boundaries and precision, that can actually be answered with data.

required_facts.statement: In the engagement and scoping stage, the analyst should engage with the commissioner to identify the question, the context, and the boundaries of the analysis, as well as constraints such as deadlines and available resources.
The engagement and scoping stage should lead to agreement between the analyst and commissioner about the outputs of the work, including acceptable levels of accuracy, precision and margins of error.

A well-formed statistical question makes clear the variable(s) of interest, the group it focuses on, and its intent — describing the data, comparing a variable across two or more groups, or looking at an association between two variables — and can be answered with data collected or already in hand.

optional_enrichment.statement: “How tall is the plant?” is answered with a single height, so it is not a statistical investigative question, unlike “Do plants exposed to more sunlight grow faster?”

briefs.learning_objective: Identify a stakeholder's requirements (scope, constraints, and expected output) before starting an analysis, and capture them in a specification.

required_facts.statement: In the engagement and scoping stage, the commissioner should inform the analyst about the important aspects of the problem, its scope, and any constraints or issues.

The analyst should create a specification document that captures the commissioner's requirements, providing a definition of the scope and project constraints; the analyst should share this specification with the commissioner for sign-off.
The commissioner should communicate to the analyst any relevant information about data sources and data quality.
Constraints around resources and timelines should be clarified and agreed between the analyst and commissioner during engagement and scoping.
The engagement and scoping stage should lead to agreement between the analyst and commissioner about the outputs of the work.

briefs.learning_objective: Write a recommendation that is explicitly grounded in, and traceable to, an analysis's specific findings.

required_facts.statement: The value of analytical efforts is only truly realized when the insights discovered are acted upon.

The example shows a 'because we found X, we recommend Y' pattern directly connecting a finding to a recommendation, for example: '...was successful and, because of the success, we recommend continuing to offer it going forward; please approve our budget for this program.'

briefs.learning_objective: Translate a technical result into a plain-language takeaway for a non-technical audience by removing or explaining jargon and preferring short, everyday words.

required_facts.statement: Specialist terms can be used where needed — they are not always jargon — but explain them in plain English the first time they appear.

Formal or long words should be avoided when an easy or short one will do (for example 'buy' instead of 'purchase', 'help' instead of 'assist', 'about' instead of 'approximately'), and jargon or buzzwords should be avoided because they are often vague and can be misinterpreted.

briefs.learning_objective: Prioritize which findings to lead with based on their relevance to the stakeholder's decision, rather than which finding is most analytically interesting.

required_facts.statement: The engagement and scoping stage of an analytical project should establish an understanding of how the analysis will inform decisions.
Crafting a communication's big idea requires knowing what is not essential, and boiling the overall message down to a single sentence that captures its core.
Writing about data should only include information relevant to the audience.
Use the inverted pyramid: the most important information should be first, and everything else arranged from most to least important.
source_refs: gov_uk_writing_about_data#Have a logical and organised structure

briefs.learning_objective: Frame a recommendation that states what action should be taken about a finding, distinct from restating the finding itself.

required_facts.statement: The value of analytical efforts is only truly realized when the insights discovered are acted upon; an audience cannot be assumed to find the intended takeaway as obvious as the presenter thinks it is.

In the example Big Idea '...was successful and, because of the success, we recommend continuing to offer it going forward; please approve our budget for this program.', it's clear to the audience what they need to know and what they are being asked to do.

briefs.learning_objective: Write an opening context section for a findings narrative that establishes why the analysis was done, before presenting any finding.

required_facts.statement: In a story's structure, the beginning establishes the context: what's happening, or what the situation is, when the story begins.
A summary should have an obvious beginning, middle, and end; in one example the beginning level-sets the audience before diving into the analysis.

A release shouldn't start with lengthy background information or technical definitions; instead it should include a short paragraph explaining what the publication is about, with more detailed information placed in a separate section.
source_refs: gov_uk_writing_about_statistics_archived#Don’t start with lengthy background information or technical definitions

required_facts.statement: Explaining why the statistics have been collected includes relevant, factual information about the policy and operational context.
source_refs: gov_uk_writing_about_statistics_archived#Explain why the statistics have been collected

briefs.learning_objective: Adjust how much technical detail to include in a presentation of the same finding, based on the audience's technical background.

required_facts.statement: While it isn't always the reality, designing with a specific person in mind as the audience can help avoid the 'mixed audience' trap; knowing the audience's motivations lets a presenter frame what they need to know or do in terms of those motivating factors.
Knowledge of the audience should inform choices such as how much information density to include, and whether to add more context or explain something in greater detail.

Technical or detail-oriented people may prefer to understand the specifics of an analysis first, so they are prepared to take in ideas about next steps; with executives or other 'big-picture'-oriented people, who do not have a lot of patience for the specifics of an analysis, you should think about starting with your request.
An executive audience might only want the high-level arc.

briefs.learning_objective: Anticipate the questions or objections a stakeholder is likely to raise about a finding or recommendation, and prepare a response in advance.

required_facts.statement: An analyst should be prepared to respond to challenge from the approver, or scrutiny from project or programme boards, about their analysis.

Technical or detail-oriented people prefer to understand the specifics of an analysis first so they are prepared to take in ideas about next steps; presenting findings before a request can, in that situation, avoid an audience derailing the presentation with a bunch of questions.
Being tailored to the audience means thinking about what questions they will ask, and answering these in the writing.

briefs.learning_objective: Match a chart type to the specific point being communicated to a stakeholder audience (trend, comparison, distribution, or part-to-whole), distinct from choosing a chart type for one's own exploration.

required_facts.statement: A bar chart is used for graphing categorical data and comparing values across categories.
Line graphs are best when you want to show how the value of something changes over time, or compare how several things change over time relative to each other.
Boxplots offer a condensed display for comparing the distributions of multiple datasets side by side.

A pie chart expresses a part-to-whole relationship in the data, and is best used either for a general sense of how parts relate to the whole, or to highlight that one segment is notably larger or smaller than the others; the pie must depict a meaningful whole (values that sum to 100%).

A boxplot may be unfamiliar to many people and could introduce a learning curve; choosing a different display altogether may avoid confusion for audiences who do not know this chart type or how to read it.
source_refs: swd_what_is_a_boxplot#When should you not use a boxplot?

required_facts.statement: A scatterplot is often used to understand data rather than to communicate with it, though it can still be designed to convey findings to an audience.

misconceptions.statement: It is just as easy to precisely compare the sizes of pie slices as it is to compare bar lengths.

briefs.learning_objective: Simplify a technical-looking chart for a non-technical audience by removing gridlines, chart borders, and unneeded label precision, without changing the underlying data.

required_facts.statement: Gridlines can be deleted from a chart; if precise values matter to the audience, label the data point(s) directly instead of relying on gridlines.
A chart's border can be removed, since it is not adding informative value; white space can differentiate parts of a visual better than a border.
Data labels should be used sparingly, only where the exact values are important to the audience; otherwise they should be removed and the axis used instead.
Reducing clutter lets the audience use their attention to decide what actions might be warranted, rather than working out how to read the graph.
Unnecessary trailing zeroes can be dropped from axis labels.
Diagonally rotated axis text is slower to read; labels can be abbreviated so they render horizontally instead.

briefs.learning_objective: Structure a short presentation of findings using an opening, body, and call-to-action, following a narrative arc from context through analysis to a takeaway.

required_facts.statement: A summary should have an obvious beginning, middle, and end; in one example, the beginning level-sets the audience, the middle presents the analysis, and the end concludes with the key takeaways.
In a story's structure, the beginning establishes the context of the situation, and this gets carried, onward and upward, to the twist, before the ending brings the story to its close.
A presentation can end with a call to action, stating what is being asked of the audience, once the audience has the context needed to understand the request.

briefs.learning_objective: Write a concise executive summary that gives a reader an analysis's main findings and recommendation without their needing to read the full report.

required_facts.statement: An executive summary is a one- or two-page overview of a much longer presentation, provided so the reader gets the main messages without reading the entire communication; it may be the only thing the audience ever looks at.
The summary's title should state the main takeaway and set the tone for the rest of the page, and the summary should follow a narrative arc with an obvious beginning, middle, and end.

Content should be grouped into easily-discernible sections with text headers, so someone scanning for only a few seconds still understands the main points; bullets should generally be avoided in favor of well-constructed sentences and mini-paragraphs, except when listing elements.

briefs.learning_objective: Define a specific business question or problem statement for a chosen dataset, so the question itself gives every later capstone step (retrieval, cleaning, analysis) a concrete target to serve.

required_facts.statement: Before analytical work begins, the question to be addressed, its context, and its boundaries should be identified.
Scoping ensures an appropriate, common understanding of the problem is defined, and that expectations are aligned with what the analysis can produce.

briefs.learning_objective: Given the capstone dataset and where it is stored, choose and justify whether to retrieve it with a SQL query, a spreadsheet import, or both.

required_facts.statement: Data that lives in a SQL database can be retrieved with a SQL query; pandas' SQL query wrappers (pandas.io.sql) facilitate this retrieval.
read_excel() reads an Excel file directly into a DataFrame.

briefs.learning_objective: Sequence and structure the capstone's stages of retrieval, cleaning, modeling, analysis, visualization, and communication into an outline before starting execution.

required_facts.statement: An analytical project is commonly structured through phases that begin with scoping the question and end with delivering and communicating the results; a phase such as scoping or design may need to be revisited if a later phase encounters changes or limitations.

Within that structure, the source data is retrieved (for example via a SQL query or a spreadsheet import), and data quality should be assessed at every stage, with quality improvements (such as cleaning) focused as early as possible.
source_refs: uk_gov_data_quality_framework#3.1 Assess data quality at all stages of the lifecycle

required_facts.statement: Where the project's data spans more than one table, the modeling stage connects related tables; relationships are what connect related information between tables.

In the delivery and communication stage, insights are communicated to the commissioner and approver (the people who need them); activities may include producing summary packs and reports, launching dashboards or websites, and presentations.

briefs.learning_objective: Combine already-learned SELECT, WHERE, JOIN, and GROUP BY into one SQL query that retrieves the specific rows, columns, and groups the capstone's business question needs.

required_facts.statement: A single SELECT statement's syntax allows a FROM clause, a WHERE clause, and a GROUP BY clause to appear together in the same query.

A join, such as an INNER JOIN, can be included in that same SELECT statement's FROM clause to combine matching rows from more than one table before the query's WHERE filtering or GROUP BY grouping is applied.

briefs.learning_objective: Apply already-learned spreadsheet formulas and PivotTables to complete the capstone project's spreadsheet-based analysis step.

required_facts.statement: A PivotTable is built by selecting the data range and inserting a PivotTable, then adding fields to it: non-numeric fields default to Rows, date/time fields to Columns, and numeric fields to Values, and fields can be dragged between these areas to rearrange the summary.
COUNTIFS(criteria_range1, criteria1, [criteria_range2, criteria2]…) applies criteria across one or more ranges and counts the cells for which all the criteria are met.

briefs.learning_objective: Apply already-learned pandas cleaning (isna/dropna/fillna) and analysis (groupby aggregation) to the capstone's own retrieved dataset.

required_facts.statement: isna() detects which values in a DataFrame are missing, and dropna() removes rows with missing values or fillna() replaces them with a specified value.

A groupby operation splits data into groups based on some criteria, applies a function independently to each group, and combines the results back into a single structure; an aggregation is a groupby operation that reduces each group to one summary value per column.

briefs.learning_objective: Connect the capstone project's own tables using the correct primary keys, foreign keys, and one-to-many relationships.

required_facts.statement: A primary key uniquely identifies each row of a table; a foreign key's values must match values appearing in some row of the table it references.

In a one-to-many relationship, one row on the 'one' side relates to many rows on the 'many' side (for example, one department has many employees); in the Customer/Order example, the foreign key CustID is placed in the Order table and must match a valid CustID in the Customer table.

briefs.learning_objective: Compute and interpret the descriptive statistics (using pandas) that support the capstone project's business question.

required_facts.statement: describe() computes a variety of summary statistics about a Series or the columns of a DataFrame.

The mean is more strongly affected by extreme observations than the median, which is more robust to them; so when the goal is to understand a typical individual value in a skewed dataset, the median can be more useful.

briefs.learning_objective: Build a coherent set of matplotlib/seaborn charts, arranged and annotated, that presents the capstone's key findings to a stakeholder audience.

required_facts.statement: fig, axs = plt.subplots(2, 2) creates one Figure containing a 2x2 grid of Axes, so several charts can share one figure.
plt.subplot(131), plt.subplot(132), and plt.subplot(133) can each hold a different chart side by side in one figure, and plt.suptitle() adds one title over the whole figure.

briefs.learning_objective: Independently carry out the capstone project's planned workflow across SQL, spreadsheet, Python/pandas, and visualization tools, without step-by-step guidance.

required_facts.statement: During the design phase, the commission is converted into an analytical plan, with some iteration expected as the solution is developed.

During the analysis phase, the planned analysis is carried out while progress and relevance are monitored, and appropriate records of the analysis conducted, changes, decisions, and assumptions made are maintained.

briefs.learning_objective: Write a narrated stakeholder summary that presents the capstone project's context, finding, and recommendation to its specific audience.

required_facts.statement: Designing a communication with a specific person in mind, even if that isn't always the reality, can help avoid treating a 'mixed audience' as one undifferentiated group; knowing what motivates that audience lets you frame what you need them to know or do in those terms.

During delivery, insights are communicated to the people who need them, sufficiently for them to determine whether the work meets their requirements; this communication can include summary packs, reports, or presentations.

A summary can follow a story structure with an obvious beginning, middle, and end: the beginning level-sets the audience with the big picture and background context, the middle presents what the analysis found, and the ending gives the key takeaway, such as a recommended next step.

optional_enrichment.statement: The recommendation can instead be placed up front, depending on the audience and relationship.

briefs.learning_objective: Produce documentation and a presentation of the finished capstone deliverable that lets someone else understand and evaluate the work without having watched it get built.

required_facts.statement: Transparency about the analytical decisions, process, limitations, and changes made at each stage should be clearly shown through documentation of the analysis, assumptions, and data, together with records of the decisions and quality-assurance checks made.
Delivery and communication activities can include producing summary packs and reports, launching dashboards or websites, and giving presentations.

optional_enrichment.statement: Sign-off then confirms that the required documentation and evidence have been captured.
